items.title: I can define classical conditioning and identify it as a behaviourist approach to learning
items.what: Classical conditioning is a process of learning through the involuntary association between a neutral stimulus and an unconditioned stimulus, resulting in a conditioned response. It is behaviourist because it focuses on observable behaviours produced by interacting with the external environment.
items.why: Correctly categorising classical conditioning as a behaviourist approach is required by the study design and is regularly tested in multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
items.example: Pavlov's dogs salivating at the sound of a bell is a behaviourist example because the learned salivation response can be directly observed and was produced by environmental stimuli, not by internal thought processes.

subtopic.name: Classical Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist approach to learning in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it produces a conditioned response on its own. The process unfolds across three stages: before conditioning, during conditioning, and after conditioning.
subtopic.why: Understanding classical conditioning explains how involuntary learned responses develop in humans and animals, from phobias and placebo effects to emotional associations. It is a foundational concept in VCE Psychology and is frequently assessed using novel scenarios in exams.

items.title: I can describe the stimuli and responses present in the before conditioning stage
items.what: In the before conditioning stage, a neutral stimulus (NS) produces no significant response, while an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) automatically produces an unconditioned response (UCR). There is no conditioned stimulus or conditioned response at this point.
items.why: Identifying what is and is not present before conditioning is essential for correctly mapping a real-world scenario onto the classical conditioning framework in exam responses.
items.example: In Pavlov's experiment before conditioning: the bell (NS) produced no significant response in the dogs, while the food (UCS) automatically caused the dogs to salivate (UCR).

subtopic.name: Classical Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist approach to learning in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it produces a conditioned response on its own. The process unfolds across three stages: before conditioning, during conditioning, and after conditioning.
subtopic.why: Understanding classical conditioning explains how involuntary learned responses develop in humans and animals, from phobias and placebo effects to emotional associations. It is a foundational concept in VCE Psychology and is frequently assessed using novel scenarios in exams.

items.title: I can describe what occurs during the during conditioning stage, including timing requirements
items.what: During conditioning, the NS is repeatedly paired with the UCS to produce the UCR. The NS must be presented first and remain until the UCS is presented within half a second. This repeated pairing is what establishes the association.
items.why: The timing detail (half a second) is a specific piece of knowledge that appears in VCAA exam questions and distinguishes a student who has studied the content carefully from one who has not.
items.example: In Pavlov's experiment, the bell (NS) was sounded first and the food (UCS) was presented directly afterwards, within half a second, repeatedly across many trials, producing salivation (UCR) each time.

subtopic.name: Classical Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist approach to learning in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it produces a conditioned response on its own. The process unfolds across three stages: before conditioning, during conditioning, and after conditioning.
subtopic.why: Understanding classical conditioning explains how involuntary learned responses develop in humans and animals, from phobias and placebo effects to emotional associations. It is a foundational concept in VCE Psychology and is frequently assessed using novel scenarios in exams.

items.title: I can describe the after conditioning stage and identify the conditioned stimulus and conditioned response
items.what: After conditioning, the former NS is now called the conditioned stimulus (CS) and produces a conditioned response (CR) on its own, without the UCS being present. The CR is similar to, but not identical in all respects to, the UCR.
items.why: The shift in terminology from NS to CS is a conceptual step many students miss; naming the stimulus correctly in relation to the stage is required for full marks in extended-response questions.
items.example: After conditioning in Pavlov's experiment, the sound of the bell alone (CS) caused the dogs to salivate (CR). The stimulus that was once neutral now reliably triggers the learned response without any food being present.

subtopic.name: Classical Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist approach to learning in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it produces a conditioned response on its own. The process unfolds across three stages: before conditioning, during conditioning, and after conditioning.
subtopic.why: Understanding classical conditioning explains how involuntary learned responses develop in humans and animals, from phobias and placebo effects to emotional associations. It is a foundational concept in VCE Psychology and is frequently assessed using novel scenarios in exams.

items.title: I can apply the three-phase model of classical conditioning to a novel scenario using correct terminology
items.what: Given a real-world example, the student can correctly identify the NS, UCS, UCR, CS, and CR across all three stages, using the phrase 'in response to' to distinguish the UCR from the CR.
items.why: Application to novel scenarios is the most common exam format for classical conditioning; being able to transfer the model to an unfamiliar context is essential for scoring well on 3-mark questions.
items.example: Millie's dog Dudley: before conditioning, taking the jacket off the hook (NS) produced no significant response; the lead being attached (UCS) automatically caused excitement and tail wagging (UCR). During conditioning, the jacket removal was repeatedly paired with the lead. After conditioning, the jacket removal alone (CS) caused Dudley to wag his tail excitedly (CR).

items.title: I can use correct abbreviations for classical conditioning terminology after writing terms in full
items.what: In exam responses, the full term must be written first, followed by its abbreviation in brackets (e.g., neutral stimulus (NS)). After this, the abbreviation alone can be used throughout the response.
items.why: VCAA marking guidelines require students to introduce abbreviations correctly; omitting the full term on first use can cost marks even if the underlying knowledge is accurate.
items.example: A correct exam sentence reads: 'The sound of the bell was the neutral stimulus (NS), which produced no significant response before conditioning. The NS was then repeatedly paired with the unconditioned stimulus (UCS) of food.'

subtopic.name: Classical Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical conditioning is a behaviourist approach to learning in which a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it produces a conditioned response on its own. The process unfolds across three stages: before conditioning, during conditioning, and after conditioning.
subtopic.why: Understanding classical conditioning explains how involuntary learned responses develop in humans and animals, from phobias and placebo effects to emotional associations. It is a foundational concept in VCE Psychology and is frequently assessed using novel scenarios in exams.

items.title: I can define operant conditioning and explain the role of each of the three phases
items.what: Operant conditioning involves three sequential phases: the antecedent (the stimulus or event that precedes and often elicits a behaviour), the behaviour (the voluntary action that occurs), and the consequence (the outcome that determines whether the behaviour is likely to recur).
items.why: Each phase has a precise definition and the ABC framework is a common mnemonic used in exams; being able to correctly identify each phase in a scenario is required for questions worth 3 or more marks.
items.example: Teaching a dog to sit: the command 'sit' is the antecedent; the dog sitting is the behaviour; giving the dog a treat afterwards is the consequence, which increases the likelihood the dog will sit on command again.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can define reinforcement and distinguish between positive and negative reinforcement
items.what: Reinforcement is any consequence that increases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring. Positive reinforcement involves adding a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour; negative reinforcement involves removing an undesirable stimulus to increase behaviour.
items.why: Students frequently confuse negative reinforcement with punishment because the word 'negative' is misread as unpleasant; understanding that both types of reinforcement increase behaviour is critical for accuracy.
items.example: Positive reinforcement: a student studies hard and receives a high mark, increasing their likelihood of studying hard again. Negative reinforcement: a person goes for a run when stressed and the stress reduces, increasing the likelihood of running when stressed again.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can define punishment and distinguish between positive and negative punishment
items.what: Punishment is any consequence that decreases the likelihood of a behaviour recurring. Positive punishment involves adding an undesirable stimulus to decrease behaviour; negative punishment (also called response cost) involves removing a desirable stimulus to decrease behaviour.
items.why: Correctly distinguishing all four consequence types is one of the most frequently tested skills in this topic, appearing in both multiple-choice and extended-response questions across multiple VCAA exams.
items.example: Positive punishment: a friend criticises you for arriving late, making you less likely to be late again. Negative punishment: a teenager has their phone taken away for bad behaviour at home, making them less likely to repeat that behaviour.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can use the add/remove and increase/decrease framework to classify all four types of consequences
items.what: In operant conditioning, 'positive' means a stimulus is added and 'negative' means a stimulus is removed. Combined with whether the consequence increases or decreases behaviour, this gives four types: positive reinforcement (add, increase), negative reinforcement (remove, increase), positive punishment (add, decrease), negative punishment (remove, decrease).
items.why: This two-axis framework allows confident classification of any consequence type even in unfamiliar scenarios; it prevents the common error of assuming 'negative' means unpleasant or 'positive' means pleasant.
items.example: A student is not allowed to attend a party (desirable stimulus removed) because of poor behaviour (behaviour to be decreased): this is negative punishment, because a desirable stimulus was removed and the intention is to decrease the behaviour.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can apply the three-phase model of operant conditioning to a novel scenario using correct terminology
items.what: Given a real-world scenario, the student can identify the antecedent, the voluntary behaviour, the consequence type, and explain how that consequence affects the future likelihood of the behaviour.
items.why: Novel scenario application is central to 3-4 mark extended response questions on operant conditioning, and students must use the precise language of the framework to earn full marks.
items.example: Bethany avoids taking the bins out each week by studying for at least one hour each night. The antecedent is the expectation of bin duty; the behaviour is studying; the consequence is the removal of the undesirable chore (negative reinforcement), which increases the likelihood she will continue studying.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can explain that behaviour in operant conditioning is voluntary, distinguishing it from classical conditioning
items.what: In operant conditioning, the behaviour phase involves voluntary actions: the learner consciously chooses to act. This is different from classical conditioning, where the conditioned response is involuntary and does not require conscious effort from the learner.
items.why: The voluntary versus involuntary distinction is a key comparison point assessed directly in questions asking students to differentiate classical and operant conditioning.
items.example: A rat pressing a lever in a Skinner box to receive food is a voluntary, operant behaviour. By contrast, a dog salivating when it hears a bell it associates with food is an involuntary, classically conditioned response.

subtopic.name: Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Operant conditioning is a three-phase behaviourist approach to learning in which a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) determines how likely a voluntary behaviour is to recur. The three phases are antecedent, behaviour, and consequence.
subtopic.why: Operant conditioning explains a wide range of intentional human and animal behaviours shaped by environmental outcomes, from study habits to discipline systems. It is assessed extensively in VCE Psychology, including scenario-based questions requiring correct identification of consequence type.

items.title: I can define observational learning and identify it as a social-cognitive approach
items.what: Observational learning is a process of learning that involves watching the behaviour of a model and the associated consequence of that behaviour. It is social-cognitive because it takes place in a social setting and involves internal cognitive processes such as memory, attention, and motivation.
items.why: Correctly identifying observational learning as social-cognitive, rather than behaviourist, distinguishes it from classical and operant conditioning and reflects a precise understanding the study design requires.
items.example: A child watching a parent cook a meal and later attempting to replicate the recipe is engaging in observational learning: the parent is the model, the child is the learner, and the process involves cognitive engagement, not just stimulus-response pairing.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can describe the attention stage and identify factors that influence whether a learner attends to a model
items.what: Attention is the first stage, in which the learner actively focuses on the model's behaviour and its consequences. Bandura identified that learners are more likely to attend to models who are liked, of high status, similar to the learner, familiar, visible, or perceived as someone whose behaviour can be imitated.
items.why: Questions often ask students to identify which stage is demonstrated by a particular feature of a scenario, and attention-related factors (such as a celebrity being the model) are commonly used as exam hooks.
items.example: An advertising campaign using a well-known celebrity to model using a perfume product increases the likelihood that viewers pay attention because the celebrity is of high status and perceived positively.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can describe the retention stage and explain what a mental representation is
items.what: Retention is the second stage, in which the learner creates a mental representation of the model's behaviour so that it can be stored in memory and accessed later when attempting to reproduce the behaviour.
items.why: Retention is distinct from attention: a learner can pay attention but fail to store the information. Questions often test whether students can identify which stage has not been met when a learner forgets what they observed.
items.example: After watching a knitting demonstration, Ester can describe what the teacher did in general but cannot recall the first few steps. This means she has partially met retention but has not fully created a complete mental representation.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can describe the reproduction stage and explain why it is often the hardest stage to achieve
items.what: Reproduction is the third stage, in which the learner must have the physical and mental capabilities to replicate the behaviour they observed. It is often the hardest stage because physical and mental capabilities can be outside the learner's control.
items.why: Understanding that reproduction depends on capability, not effort or desire, helps students correctly identify cases where a learner fails at reproduction despite succeeding at all other stages.
items.example: Fab watched a knitting demonstration carefully and remembered all the steps (attention and retention met), but injured his wrist prior and cannot move his left hand. He cannot meet reproduction regardless of his motivation.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can describe the motivation stage and distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
items.what: Motivation is the fourth stage, in which the learner must want to reproduce the observed behaviour. Intrinsic motivation comes from within (e.g., personal desire to improve), while extrinsic motivation comes from external factors (e.g., wanting praise or a reward).
items.why: Distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic motivation is directly testable and students must apply this distinction to scenarios to justify which type of motivation is present.
items.example: Rick wants to learn to knit because his mother has asked him to make a scarf for his grandmother's birthday. This is extrinsic motivation because the driving force comes from an external expectation rather than from Rick's own internal desire.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can describe the reinforcement stage and distinguish between self-reinforcement, external reinforcement, and vicarious reinforcement
items.what: Reinforcement is the fifth and final stage, occurring after the learner performs the behaviour. It involves receiving a positive consequence that makes the learner more likely to repeat the behaviour. It can be self-reinforcement (internal pride), external reinforcement (an award or praise), or vicarious reinforcement (observing someone else being reinforced for the same behaviour).
items.why: Vicarious reinforcement in particular is frequently assessed because it is unique to observational learning and demonstrates that reinforcement does not have to be direct to influence behaviour.
items.example: Camila watches her mother compliment her older sister Daniella for applying makeup well. Camila has not been praised herself, but observing her sister's reinforcement motivates Camila to learn makeup. This is vicarious reinforcement.

subtopic.name: Observational Learning
subtopic.what: Observational learning is a social-cognitive approach to learning in which a learner watches a model perform a behaviour and its associated consequence, then may reproduce that behaviour themselves. Learning occurs through five sequential stages: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and reinforcement.
subtopic.why: Observational learning explains how complex social behaviours, skills, and norms are acquired indirectly, without direct conditioning. The five-stage model is assessed frequently in VCE Psychology, particularly through scenarios requiring students to identify which stages a learner has or has not met.

items.title: I can identify at what point the learner performs the behaviour within the five stages
items.what: The learner does not perform the behaviour until after the first four stages (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation) have been met. Reinforcement is the only stage that occurs after the learner has performed the behaviour.
items.why: This sequencing detail is tested directly in questions asking students to place stages in order or explain why a learner cannot yet reproduce a behaviour.
items.example: Isabel watches Tarsh kick a football (attention), forms a mental image of the technique (retention), is physically capable of kicking (reproduction), and wants to join Tarsh's game (motivation). Only after Isabel actually attempts the kick does reinforcement occur, such as when Tarsh praises her.

items.title: I can explain what is meant by systems of knowledge in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander learning
items.what: Systems of knowledge refers to the way knowledge and skills in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities are based on interconnected social, physical, and spiritual understandings that inform survival and contribute to a strong sense of identity. These systems are developed communally, informed by culture and spirituality, and are highly relevant to day-to-day life.
items.why: The concept of systems of knowledge is a key term in the study design and is assessed in questions asking students to define or explain this idea with reference to what it includes.
items.example: When learning to hunt kangaroos, a learner would not study hunting techniques in isolation. Instead, they would simultaneously learn about the kangaroo's behaviour patterns, the plants it eats, its predators, its role in the ecosystem, and the cultural significance of the animal, all as an interconnected system.

subtopic.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Approaches to Learning
subtopic.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning situate the learner within a complex, interconnected system of knowledge that is multimodal, relational, and patterned on Country. Learning is not isolated to a classroom but is embedded in community, family, culture, and the land itself.
subtopic.why: This topic requires students to understand a fundamentally different framework for conceptualising learning, one that contrasts with individualist Western models. It is assessed in the VCE study design and requires students to describe, apply, and evaluate these approaches in written responses.

items.title: I can explain what Country means in the context of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander learning
items.what: Country refers to the traditional lands of a particular language or cultural group, including not just geographical boundaries but also the spiritual, emotional, and intellectual connections to and within those lands. Learning is patterned on Country, meaning knowledge is inherently tied to the place it belongs to.
items.why: Country is a term used with a capital C by convention to distinguish it from the common noun 'country', and understanding its full meaning, including spiritual and relational dimensions, is required for accurate exam responses.
items.example: Learning the rules of netball would make little sense on a football field; similarly, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge is deeply connected to the specific land it comes from, and learning is most meaningful when embedded in that place.

subtopic.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Approaches to Learning

It is assessed in the VCE study design and requires students to describe, apply, and evaluate these approaches in written responses.

items.title: I can explain what is meant by multimodal learning in the context of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches
items.what: Multimodal means that learning uses a variety of methods simultaneously, including story-sharing, learning maps, non-verbal communication (such as dance and art), symbols and images, land links, non-linear thinking, deconstruct/reconstruct, and community links. These are codified in the 8 ways of Aboriginal learning framework.
items.why: Students are required to identify and explain elements of the 8 ways framework in exam questions, and must be able to describe what each element involves and give a relevant example.
items.example: In a traditional dance where movements replicate the patterns of a particular animal, learners acquire knowledge about that animal's behaviour through a non-verbal mode of learning, while also participating in a cultural ceremony that connects them to community and Country.

subtopic.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Approaches to Learning
subtopic.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning situate the learner within a complex, interconnected system of knowledge that is multimodal, relational, and patterned on Country. Learning is not isolated to a classroom but is embedded in community, family, culture, and the land itself.
subtopic.why: This topic requires students to understand a fundamentally different framework for conceptualising learning, one that contrasts with individualist Western models. It is assessed in the VCE study design and requires students to describe, apply, and evaluate these approaches in written responses.

items.title: I can name and briefly describe at least four elements of the 8 ways of Aboriginal learning framework
items.what: The 8 ways framework includes: story-sharing (learning through narrative), learning maps (visual planning of knowledge), non-verbal (dance, art, observation), symbols and images (learning through imagery and metaphor), land links (knowledge connected to nature and Country), non-linear (thinking from multiple viewpoints), deconstruct/reconstruct (breaking down and rebuilding concepts), and community links (connecting learning to community needs).
items.why: Questions may ask students to identify which element of the framework is demonstrated in a given scenario, so familiarity with all eight is necessary for accurate responses.
items.example: Nullah listens to an Elder narrate the story of Tiddalik the Frog to learn how the land was formed: this reflects the story-sharing element. Kirra participates in a community dance that reenacts cultural history: this reflects the non-verbal element.

items.title: I can explain how learning is embedded in relationships in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
items.what: Learning in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities is embedded in relationships between concepts, between learner and teacher, between individuals and their families and communities, and between all of these and Country. Learning is intergenerational, family-based, and requires familiarity and trust between teacher and learner.
items.why: The relational dimension of learning is a separate and equally important part of the study design dot point; responses that only describe multimodal methods without addressing relationships will be incomplete.
items.example: In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, Elders, Aunties, and Uncles serve as knowledge-holders and teachers, passing cultural knowledge and skills to younger generations through sustained relationships built on respect and trust, rather than through a formal curriculum delivered to strangers.

subtopic.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Approaches to Learning
subtopic.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning situate the learner within a complex, interconnected system of knowledge that is multimodal, relational, and patterned on Country. Learning is not isolated to a classroom but is embedded in community, family, culture, and the land itself.
subtopic.why: This topic requires students to understand a fundamentally different framework for conceptualising learning, one that contrasts with individualist Western models. It is assessed in the VCE study design and requires students to describe, apply, and evaluate these approaches in written responses.

items.title: I can explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning differ from behaviourist and social-cognitive approaches
items.what: Unlike behaviourist approaches that focus on stimulus-response associations, or social-cognitive approaches that focus on internal cognitive processes during observation, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches situate the learner within a whole system: knowledge is holistic, relational, land-based, spiritual, and communal rather than individualistic or mechanistic.
items.why: Cross-topic comparison questions require students to articulate what is distinctive about each approach to learning, and the systems-based nature of First Nations approaches is the key differentiating feature.
items.example: Classical conditioning explains a specific learned response to a stimulus in isolation. By contrast, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander learning would connect that same stimulus to its ecological, cultural, spiritual, and community context simultaneously, treating knowledge as a web rather than a chain.

subtopic.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Approaches to Learning
subtopic.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander approaches to learning situate the learner within a complex, interconnected system of knowledge that is multimodal, relational, and patterned on Country. Learning is not isolated to a classroom but is embedded in community, family, culture, and the land itself.
subtopic.why: This topic requires students to understand a fundamentally different framework for conceptualising learning, one that contrasts with individualist Western models. It is assessed in the VCE study design and requires students to describe, apply, and evaluate these approaches in written responses.

items.title: I can identify the key similarities between classical conditioning and operant conditioning
items.what: Both classical and operant conditioning are behaviourist approaches to learning, both involve three sequential phases, and both require repeated trials for learning to occur. Neither approach attributes learning to internal thought processes; both focus on observable behaviour shaped by the external environment.
items.why: Questions that ask for similarities are just as common as those asking for differences, and students who only memorise differences will be unable to answer these correctly.
items.example: In both Pavlov's dog experiment and a dog being trained to sit with treats, multiple repeated pairings or consequences were needed before the dog reliably displayed the learned behaviour.

subtopic.name: Comparing Classical and Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical and operant conditioning are both behaviourist three-phase approaches to learning, but they differ in the type of behaviour learned (involuntary versus voluntary), the role of the learner (passive versus active), and the mechanism of learning (stimulus association versus consequence).
subtopic.why: Comparison questions appear regularly in VCAA exams and require students to articulate both similarities and differences with precision; confusing the mechanisms of each approach is a common source of lost marks.

items.title: I can explain the key difference between the type of behaviour learned in each approach
items.what: Classical conditioning results in an involuntary learned response: the learner has no conscious control over the conditioned response. Operant conditioning results in a voluntary learned behaviour: the learner consciously acts and the consequence shapes whether they act that way again.
items.why: The involuntary/voluntary distinction is the most fundamental difference between the two approaches and is tested in both multiple-choice and short-answer questions.
items.example: Samia sweating when she tries on a new apron at a store is involuntary (classical conditioning). Bethany choosing to study to avoid taking out the bins is voluntary (operant conditioning).

subtopic.name: Comparing Classical and Operant Conditioning
subtopic.what: Classical and operant conditioning are both behaviourist three-phase approaches to learning, but they differ in the type of behaviour learned (involuntary versus voluntary), the role of the learner (passive versus active), and the mechanism of learning (stimulus association versus consequence).
subtopic.why: Comparison questions appear regularly in VCAA exams and require students to articulate both similarities and differences with precision; confusing the mechanisms of each approach is a common source of lost marks.

items.title: I can explain the difference in the role of the learner across the two approaches
items.what: The learner is passive during classical conditioning: they do not consciously choose to produce the conditioned response. The learner is active during operant conditioning: they voluntarily produce a behaviour that is then shaped by its consequence.
items.why: Passive versus active is a direct point of comparison assessed in the study design and in VCAA exam questions asking students to compare the two approaches.
items.example: In Little Albert's case, the infant did not choose to fear the white rat; the fear response was passively conditioned. In contrast, a student who starts studying more because they receive good marks for effort is actively altering their behaviour based on a consequence.

items.title: I can link the type of behaviour in each conditioning approach to the division of the nervous system involved
items.what: Classical conditioning typically involves the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary responses of visceral muscles, organs, and glands. Operant conditioning typically involves the somatic nervous system, which coordinates voluntary movement of skeletal muscles.
items.why: This cross-topic link to the nervous system is explicitly noted in the study design lesson links and appears in multi-part questions combining content from different areas of the course.
items.example: Salivation (classical conditioning, Pavlov's dogs) is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Pressing a lever to receive food (operant conditioning, Skinner box) is a voluntary movement controlled by the somatic nervous system.

items.title: I can identify that operant conditioning requires a consequence while classical conditioning does not
items.what: A defining feature of operant conditioning is that a consequence (reinforcement or punishment) must follow the behaviour for learning to occur. Classical conditioning does not involve any consequence; instead, learning occurs through the repeated pairing of two stimuli.
items.why: Students sometimes incorrectly apply consequence-based reasoning to classical conditioning scenarios, so being clear that consequences are absent from classical conditioning prevents this error.
items.example: Dudley the dog wagging his tail at the sound of a jacket being removed did not require any reward or punishment; the association between the sound (NS) and the walk (UCS) was sufficient. No consequence was delivered to Dudley for his tail-wagging behaviour.
